claims.text: A defect-aware, multi-temperature, multi-fidelity machine-learning model will predict conductivity of oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than standard perfect-crystal analytical methods.
The model's improved agreement will extend across both the nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
The target material is polycrystalline HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
This oxygen-containing polycrystalline material represents a defect-containing, realistically processed composition.

The proposed model will incorporate descriptors of oxygen-induced scattering and local structural distortion and will be trained using first-principles data and partial experimental conductivity measurements.
Predictions and measurements will cover nearly 0–200 K and 300–1200 K on the same specimen containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Interstitial oxygen produces point defects and local structural non-idealities in HfNbTaTiZr.
Electron and phonon scattering contributions to transport vary across temperature regimes.
Oxygen point defects and local structural non-idealities alter electron and phonon scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Learning defect-scattering contributions over multiple temperature regimes will correct the oversimplified perfect-crystal assumptions of existing analytical models.
Explicitly capturing oxygen-doping effects on conduction pathways will improve agreement with measured conductivity.
The model will reduce conductivity prediction error from approximately 10–15% to below approximately 5%.
The largest accuracy advantage will occur at low and intermediate temperatures where defect scattering is prominent.
Established analytical formulas for HfNbTaTiZr are based on defect-free, single-phase material.
Existing analytical methods fail to capture defect and dopant effects and have errors greater than 10% against experiment.
The proposed model is restricted to HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen and temperatures from 0 K to 1200 K.
Predictions for other oxygen levels or temperatures above 1200 K are uncertain without additional data.
Differences in microstructure or oxygen distribution from the training data may change the model's quantitative accuracy improvement.
Conductivity measurements from 600–800 K on the same oxygen-containing specimen will be withheld from training and used as a benchmark.
A deviation greater than approximately 5% between predicted and measured held-out conductivity will falsify the hypothesis.
